title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Maya Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance targets, and key architecture decision records (ADRs). It is intended as the primary reference for engineers and architects designing services or components that will run on the Redwood platform or integrate with customer-facing inference APIs.

Scope and goals
- Provide a single, opinionated set of standards that balance developer productivity with production reliability and observability.
- Reduce accidental divergence between teams by specifying required configuration, SLOs, and ownership.
- Document recent ADRs that materially affect platform architecture and developer-facing contracts.

Principles
1. Backward-compatibility by default: explicit, dated breaking-change policy when compatibility cannot be maintained.
2. Observable-by-design: every service must emit metrics, structured logs, and traces for all user-facing flows.
3. Cost-aware engineering: latency, token-cost, and GPU utilization should be first-class considerations for model-serving components.
4. Minimum viable complexity: prefer simple, testable solutions over architectural novelty.

1) API standards
Purpose: Ensure consistent, discoverable, and stable HTTP/SDK contracts for all Redwood APIs (internal and external).
Required conventions:
- API surface and spec: all public and internal APIs must provide an OpenAPI v3 YAML file stored in the repo under /api/openapi.yaml and published to our internal spec registry.
- Naming and paths: use plural nouns for resources (e.g., /models, /deployments), version in the path for breaking changes (/v1/...).
- Versioning policy: semantic versioning for SDKs; API path versioning for breaking changes. Deprecated endpoints must include a deprecation header (X-Deprecation-Info) with removal date.
- Authentication: Bearer tokens via Authorization header for internal services; mutual TLS required for private deployment control-plane endpoints.
- Error handling: use structured error objects with fields: code, message, details (optional). Map HTTP codes consistently: 400 validation, 401 auth, 403 authorization, 404 not found, 429 rate limit, 5xx server errors.
- Rate limiting & quotas: upstream gateway enforces per-token and per-account quotas. Default burst policy: 200 rps per account with a sustained 50 rps if unqualified; Dedicated customers require custom quotas.
- Schema stability: changes that add optional fields are backward-compatible. Removing/renaming fields requires an ADR and 30 days of announced deprecation.

Example API fragment (OpenAPI):

  components:
    schemas:
      GenerationRequest:
        type: object
        properties:
          model:
            type: string
          prompt:
            type: string
          max_tokens:
            type: integer

2) Coding standards
Supported languages: primary services should be written in Go (gRPC/HTTP) or TypeScript (frontend and orchestrators). Python is acceptable for research and evaluation tooling but must include typed interfaces and strict linting for production code.
Requirements:
- Formatting & linting: gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, eslint + Prettier for TypeScript, black + ruff for Python. Commits must pass pre-commit hooks.
- Testing: unit tests for all modules; integration tests for critical flows. Target >= 80% coverage for service library code.
- PRs and reviews: PR size limit ~400 lines of change; require at least one cross-team reviewer for infra or API changes.
- Documentation: public functions and APIs must include docstrings; services must include a README with deployment, required env vars, and observability hooks.
- Secrets handling: never commit secrets; use vault-backed secrets manager and env-injection via runtime templating.

3) Infrastructure standards
IaC and deployments:
- Terraform modules: all cloud resources created using our standardized Terraform modules in infra/modules. Modules must include tagging (team, cost_center, owner) and a change approval checklist.
- Network topology: production services must run in regional VPCs with private subnets for compute nodes and NAT egress. Internal-only control-plane endpoints are restricted to customer VPC or private peering.
- Secrets & keys: KMS for envelope encryption; HSM for private deployments that require FIPS keys.
- CI/CD: all deployments must be automated via our GitHub Actions pipelines and gate on integration tests and canary analysis.
- Naming & tagging: resource names must follow: <env>-<team>-<service>-<component>. Tag keys: team, owner, cost_center, project.

4) Model-serving standards
Objective: reliable, low-latency inference with reproducible model versions and safe fallbacks.
Requirements:
- Model packaging: every model in the catalog must include a manifest (model.manifest.json) with fields: model_id, version, architecture, tokenizer_version, quantization_profile, tested_sequence_length, owner. Manifests are stored in the model registry.
- Quantization profiles: supported profiles documented in /applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles. Each profile must list expected latency reduction, memory footprint, and observed quality delta.
- Variant strategy: require a primary (high-accuracy) and fallback (low-latency/quantized) variant for customer-facing endpoints. Routing policies must be codified in the deployment descriptor.
- KV cache & prefix caching: runtime must declare the expected cache keys; services should opt into prefix caching via manifest flag.
- Rollouts and canaries: deployments must use staged rollouts with a default 5% canary for 30 minutes, automatic rollback if latency or error-rate thresholds exceed configured limits.
- Model change testing: every model update must include automated evals (prompt-set based) and a quality regression check in Redwood Optimize before rollout.

5) Observability standards
All services and model-serving components must be instrumented according to the following minimal signal set: metrics, structured logs, and distributed traces.
- Metrics (Prometheus format):
  - request_latency_seconds (histogram) by route, model_id, region
  - request_success_total, request_error_total by code, route, model_id
  - token_generated_total by model_id and route
  - gpu_utilization_percent by node-pool
- Logs: structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, trace_id, span_id, svc, env, msg, context (map). Sensitive fields must be redacted before ingestion.
- Tracing: follow OpenTelemetry conventions; trace IDs must be propagated between API gateway, runtime, and backend services.
- Dashboards & alerts: every service must ship a baseline dashboard with latency p50/p95/p99, error rate, and saturation metrics. Pager alerting for SLO breaches and sustained high error rate (>5% over 5m).

SLO table (required baseline):

| Signal | Target | Alert threshold |
|--------|--------|----------------|
| API availability (5m rolling) | 99.95% | < 99.9% triggers page |
| Median request latency (p50) | < 120 ms (hosted API) | p50 > 200 ms for 10m |
| p95 request latency | < 500 ms (hosted API) | p95 > 1s for 10m |
| Model correctness (eval pass rate) | >= 99% on core prompt sets | drop > 1% vs baseline triggers triage |

6) Performance standards and benchmarking
- Benchmark harness: use the eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite to run nightly perf suites across representative models and sequence-length distributions.
- Load testing: synthetic load tests for new capacity and autoscaling policies. For Dedicated pools, validate throughput at 1.5x expected peak before accepting capacity changes.
- Profiling and optimization: per-release profiling report required for changes that touch the runtime. Include kernel-level breakdowns when GPU-bound.
- Cost/perf trade-offs: every model variant must include an expected cost-per-token estimate in the manifest; Optimize recommendations must be followed for high-volume workloads.

7) Decision records (ADRs) - summary
This section records key architecture decisions that affect developers and platform behavior. Each entry below references the canonical ADR stored in /architecture-and-standards/decision-records.
- ADR-2026-01: Standardize on OpenAPI v3 for external and internal APIs. Owner: Ethan Park. Rationale: Single source of truth for SDK generation and contract tests.
- ADR-2026-02: Runtime fallback strategy: require a quantized fallback for cost-sensitive tiers. Owner: Priya Mehta. Rationale: Improve availability and cost predictability.
- ADR-2026-03: Adopt mutual TLS for private control-plane endpoints. Owner: Sarah Li. Rationale: Customer security requirements and auditability.
- ADR-2026-04: Default p95 latency SLO of 500ms for hosted inference v1. Owner: Javier Morales. Rationale: Market expectation for interactive experiences; adjusted in 2026-09 per load results.

8) Operational runbook (high-level steps for a model-serving incident)
1. Triage: confirm scope (accounts, regions, models) and mark incident in PagerDuty; set incident commander.
2. Mitigation: if latency or error-rate spikes, trigger automated fallback to quantized variant and shift traffic to healthy region.
3. Diagnostics: collect traces, top-10 slow endpoints, GPU utilization, recent deploys, and model manifest versions.
4. Rollback/patch: if deploy suspected, rollback to last known good revision; if model quality regression, switch to previous model version and initiate quality triage.
5. Postmortem: publish within 72 hours with timeline, root cause, corrective action, and owner for each action item.

Ownership and governance
- Standards owner: Architecture & Standards working group (rotating chairs from eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime).
- Exceptions and changes: changes to these standards require an ADR. Minor clarifications can be merged by the standards owner; breaking policy changes require a formal ADR and reviewer sign-off (security, platform, and a customer-facing product representative).

Appendices
A. Links and artifacts
- Model registry: /applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding
- Quantization profiles: /applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles
- Benchmark suite: /eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- ADR directory: /architecture-and-standards/decision-records

B. Quick checklist for new services (must be included in PR template)
- [ ] OpenAPI spec in /api/openapi.yaml
- [ ] README with env vars and observability links
- [ ] Metrics instrumented per metrics spec
- [ ] Baseline dashboard created and linked
- [ ] Terraform module and tagging compliant
- [ ] Model manifest (if applicable) and automated evals configured

For questions or to propose an exception, contact the Architecture & Standards working group via #arch-standards on Slack or open an ADR in the /architecture-and-standards/decision-records directory.
